scenes.title: Change the question, the winner changes
scenes.sub: Same category, different question: the brand AI recommends changes
items: McDonald's · “Which fast food place has the best fries?”
McDonald's · “Which fast food chain has the best burger?”
scenes.say: Ask AI where to get fast food, and there's no single right answer. How you phrase the question changes the winner. Ask which place has the best fries, and McDonald's is recommended in five of six answers. Ask which chain has the best burger, and McDonald's is recommended in none. Across eight questions, five different chains came out on top. We ran these measurements in November. In this video, we look at how this plays out for fast food and smart rings, which websites the AIs read, and how you can see which questions your brand is losing.

scenes.title: Winner by question
rows: Best cheap meal deal right now
scenes.note: 6 answers per question (3 AIs × 2), limited sample. Gemini (from memory) returned too few answers to show.
scenes.say: Here's how we measured. We asked eight real buyer questions from the US, with no brand names in them. ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity answered each one twice using live web search, so six answers per question. The results: for the best burger, Five Guys. For the best chicken sandwich, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes. Customer service and best chain in America, Chick-fil-A. Best fries and the best cheap meal deal right now, McDonald's. For a road trip stop, In-N-Out. Six answers per question is a limited sample, but the pattern is clear: a few words in the question change the winner.

scenes.title: Same brand, very different results
scenes.sub: Answers recommending McDonald's (6 live answers per question)
scenes.note: All 48 live answers: Chick-fil-A 23 · In-N-Out 14 · McDonald's 13 · Five Guys 11
scenes.say: Let's zoom in on one brand. McDonald's was recommended in five of six answers about fries and about value meal deals, and in three about road trips. But for the best burger, the best chicken sandwich, customer service, the healthiest chain, and even the best chain in America, it was recommended zero times. Overall, thirteen of forty-eight answers. Chick-fil-A led with twenty-three. Our read: the AIs seem to tie McDonald's to price and fries, not to quality or service. That's an observation from the answers; we can't say for sure why.

scenes.title: Smart rings: same story
scenes.sub: Answers recommending Oura, US (6 live answers per question)
rows: Best ring to buy this Black Friday
scenes.say: This isn't just fast food. For smart rings in the US, Oura was recommended in all six answers for sleep tracking, fitness, gifts, and the best ring to buy this Black Friday. But add the words no monthly subscription, and Oura drops to zero; RingConn and Samsung Galaxy Ring take six of six. Ask about battery life: Oura zero, Ultrahuman six. Ask for an affordable ring: Oura two, RingConn six. One feature word in the question, and the leader is gone. Our read: when the question names a feature, the AIs seem to recommend whoever is known for that feature, and overall popularity doesn't carry over.

scenes.title: Where does AI look?
scenes.sub: Smart rings, US · line = answers citing that site and mentioning the brand
scenes.note: Brands' own sites as sources (48 answers): ringconn.com 4 · ultrahuman.com 4 · ouraring.com 2
scenes.say: So where do the AIs look when they answer? The most cited sites are review publishers: Tom's Guide, TechRadar, Wired and Wareable. Then come two brand sites: RingConn's and Ultrahuman's own pages were each cited in four of forty-eight answers. Oura's own site, in two. Those are exactly the brands that won the battery and subscription questions. The AIs appear to combine a few review lists with brand pages to build each answer. A brand's own page being cited doesn't guarantee a recommendation, but it suggests that a clear page answering the exact question can help.

scenes.say: How do you see this for your own brand? The Conditional Visibility Map in our dashboard groups your questions by what the customer is doing: comparing options, ready to buy, researching, and so on. For each group, it shows your recommendation rate, a confidence range, and the competitor recommended most in that group. Real example: in the McDonald's measurement, comparison questions recommended McDonald's in eight of thirty-six answers, and the top competitor there was Chick-fil-A. Ready-to-buy questions: five of twelve. Groups under twenty answers are flagged, so you don't draw conclusions from a small sample. You can also tag your questions, like budget, premium, or a country, and compare the same way by tag.

scenes.title: Which question is your brand losing?
scenes.sub: Independent measurement · Not representative of the whole market · No brand partnerships
points: Don't measure with one question: ask about price, quality and features separately.
For each question you lose, find who wins and which sites the AI reads.
Publish a page that answers that exact question, then measure again in a few weeks.
scenes.say: So what should you do? One: don't measure your brand with a single question; ask about price, quality and features separately. Two: for each question you lose, find out who wins and which sites the AI is reading. Three: publish a page that answers that exact question, and measure again in a few weeks.
